Snake Carcass was found next east edge line and south of Twy G on Rwy 19L during inspection. No strikes were reported. I m not sure if a plane ran over the snake or if was just attacked by a bird or something. Again, no strike was reported. EMAIL UPDATE FROM M TRIPP ON 4/4/22 STATED THAT THEY THOUGHT THE SNAKE WEIGHTED MUCH MORE THATN 2.2 LBS. I do not know the type of snake, but during a runway inspection, I found part of the snake on the centerline, with the rest (and most) of the body toward the runway edge line. The only reason I added this to the FAA Strike Report database is that the advisory circular mentions that a reptile over 1kg (2.2 lbs) and if it was found within 250 ft of the centerline should be entered into the database. When I collected the snake remains, the snake felt much heavier than 2-3 pounds. I didn t have a scale with me, but I m certain the snake weighed more than the 1kg/2.2 lbs mentioned in the advisory circular.

NTSB CEN24LA229     At approximately, 15:55 CDT I was finishing my last clean up pass on field number 5, heading South West. As I was pulling out of the field a flock of ducks flew up in front of me. I applied a little more pressure to the stick to climb above the ducks but it was not enough and I came in contact with some of them. At this time, I was approximately 30ft off the ground. Initially thinking the ducks ended up in my spray gear and the main landing gear I continued my climb in order to clear the shelterbelt and the pole line on the south end of the field. A few seconds after contact with the ducks, I felt the engine quit producing thrust. I verified this by checking my engine gauges and witnessing the N1, torque, and EGT gauges rolling back. I pushed my power lever forward to verify the engine had in fact quit as it had no effect. At this time, I am approximately 80 ft above ground. Having no altitude and running out of airspeed, my only option was to land straight ahead. I pitched the aircraft down to gain a little more airspeed and when I was just over the ground I put the aircraft into a three-point landing configuration. I did not use flaps. As the aircraft came into contact with the ground, the main landing gear sank into the wet ground, as we had a good rain shower that morning. The aircraft then flipped on its back. At the time, I had 20 gallons of product on board and approximately 90 gallons of fuel. When everything quit moving I exited the aircraft as quickly as possible. TWO PHOTOS. NON-DAMAGING STRIKE REPORT / POST STRIKE INVESTIGATION:  A Wildlife Officer reported to the gate of an American Airlines aircraft after notification of bird remains found on the aircraft. Upon arrival at the gate the AAL mechanic indicated to the right landing gear where bird remains were found between the landing gear door and the strut. The Wildlife Officer was able to remove the partial remains of what may be a gull. The remains were very dry and no other signs of the strike were visible on the aircraft. The Wildlife Officer interviewed the flight crew and was told by the first officer, that she found the bird remains while conducting a pre-flight check of the aircraft. It seems the strike was experienced by the prior crew and flight, but nothing was written up in the cockpit log by the previous crew, indicating that they might not have noticed they had struck a but most likely on take-off from their previous destination of RDU. Shortly after seeing the birds, we heard a noise from above. As we were already in a downwind position for RWY 31, we opted to request a precautionary landing from the Salinas tower. COMMENTS: database note: originally entered as Found KATL. Changed to Departure DNMM per email from RD on 11.21.22: As outlined in email on 18 Jul 2021 (see below), I recommend that this strike (2021-06-29-094742) be updated to occurring on Departure at DNMM (Nigeria) on 16 June 2021 from the presently entered Unknown airport (ZZZZ) on 18 June 2021. The species was IDed by SFL and this is the only reasonable scenario as the aircraft had a nighttime departure from DNMM (where the tomb bat lives) on 16 June for KATL (it had landed at DNMM during daytime) and was in USA until 18 June (2 days later) when bat was discovered on the aircraft in ATL (and sent to SFL where it was IDed as Mauritian tomb bat).   Thanks to Delta Maintenance and SFL, we now can reasonably assume that this strike occurred during nighttime Departure at DNMM on 16 June 2021. This would not have been an âEnroute strikeâ as this is not a migratory bat and would have been very unlikely to be flying at any significant height AGL. Thus, this bat was struck at night on departure from DNMM on 16 June and the snarge stayed under left wing for 2 days before discovery during which N854NW flew to ATL, ATL to SLC, SLC to ATL, ATL to DTW, and DTW to ATL.

MOR Remarks: JBU1205 departed Rwy10L. One mile later, he said he thinks he may have blown a tire and that we should inspect the runway. We called Airfield to come out for inspection on 10L, as Tracon informed us to hold departures, that JBU was coming back to land. Airfield found "bird and fine tire debri" and closed Rwy10L. The crash units were called to respond and positioned themselves at 10R. JBU1205 held to the West for about 45 minutes, during which they requested more detail on the debri. Airfield, who had left 10L to join the response at 10R, went back to 10L to furher research the debri. It was now being reported as bird only. JBU1205 landed on RWY10R at 0658Z. Airfield inspected 10R behind his arrival and found a 2x3" piece of carbon fiber with bird debri on it. Other Remarks: The crew felt the impact but did not know it was a bird, they believed it was a blown tire. JetBlue 1206 had ingested a large bird that went through the fan section of the right engine creating thousands of small bird debris on the runway right after takeoff. They flew to an area northwest of the airport and remained on station for an hour so they could burn fuel, and go through checklists. Unfortunately, A320 aircraft cannot tell what their tire pressure is so they were not sure until after visual confirmation that they most likely did not have a blown tire. The passengers were provided hotel accommodations and have been rescheduled on a rescue flight coming from Long Beach at 0930 today for a rescheduled departure of 1134. No negative feedback was received from customers aboard the aircraft. There was a 6-8 inch hole in the leading edge of the right flap and a 12 inch dent in the cowling of the right engine. The bird had been ingested in the fan only with no obvious signs that it went into the core but more to follow after a scope. Aircraft is still out of service. 11/29/2018  Remains pulled from hole in flap of right wing positively identified as Canada goose. Photos of remains available by contacting reporter below. Remains from engine still to be determined by Smithsonian. Video of the strike shows strike occurred AT LEAST AT 80  AGL

On Thursday, July 24th, 2025, I was conducting a routine perimeter inspection of the AOA when I overheard the crew of Endeavor Airlines dba Delta Connection flight #4973 report striking a bird on its windshield during its take-off run on runway 36 at approximately 11:35 AM local time. I performed an inspection of runway 36 beginning at the approach end and located the remains of a barn swallow right of runway centerline just past the taxiway M4 exit, approximately 3000 feet from the beginning of the runway. The remains showed signs of trauma consistent with striking an aircraft and blood splatter was present on the runway underneath the remains. I removed the remains from the runway and took several feathers and DNA samples for submission to the Smithsonian before disposing of the remains. Nothing further to report. Flight continued as normal to DTW.

JetBlue FLT 1411 reported a bird strike on departure to ATC. The flight returned to FLL for a precautionary landing to have maintenance inspect the aircraft. Airport operations inspected runway 28L but no remains were found. The pilot stated the strike occurred about 0.5 miles west of the airfield over I-95 at about 700 ft. AGL. There was a dent in the fuselage above the pilot s window near the cabin door, but very little blood or snarge was present. The area was wiped with alcohol swabs and sent to the Smithsonian for ID. The pilot saw at least two large birds that may have been vultures. JetBlue conducted an aircraft swap and FLT 1411 departed at 1352 local (2 hour and 14 minute delay). N640JB is currently on a remote parking spot being inspected by JetBlue maintenance. TWO PHOTOS. Update: Per JetBlue Maintenance, the dent to the fuselage was within acceptable limits. The aircraft departed at 0931 local the next day with passengers (1/28/22). Aircraft OTS approximately 21 hours. MOR: JBU1411 HAD A BIRD STRIKE AFTER DEPARTING RWY 28L. JBU1411 DID NOT DECLARE AN EMERGENCY BUT WANTED TO RETURN TO FLL. AIRCRAFT WAS RESEQUENCED BY MIA APPROACH AND LANDED AT 1707Z. AFTER INSPECTION OF THE AIRCRAFT BCAD INFORMED US THAT THERE WAS A DENT IN THE FUSELAGE ABOVE THE CAPTAINS WINDOW AND THE AIRCRAFT WOULD BE TAKEN OUT OF SERVICE. DEN, ROC AND ATM WERE NOTIFIED. AN 8020-9 FORM WAS EMAILED IN TO THE ROC. Smithsonian Wildlife/Species Identification: Black vulture (Coragyps atratus)

DAMAGING STRIKE REPORT / POST STRIKE INVESTIGATION:  A Wildlife Officer reported to the AAL maintenance hangar after being notified of an aircraft taken out of service due to a bird strike. The call was received more than two hours after the aircraft had landed. According to the AAL maintenance Lead, the bird strike was noticed by the outbound flight crew during the pre-flight inspection walk-around. A very large smudge of blood was noticed on the cowling of the #2 engine. The aircraft was immediately taken out of service for further inspection. Aircraft was out for 24 hours before it returned to the flight line. It is unknown where the strike occurred, since the arrival crew never indicated a bird strike in the cockpit log or mentioned it to maintenance personnel. The lack of bird remains reported or found on the arrival runway, points to the STRIKE TAKING PLACE OFF AIRPORT PROPERTY. MEDICAL TRANSPORT. On the morning of October 3, the crew and I were returning to our base at banner Lassen in Susanville CA, from Reno NV. The time was 0011, the sky was clear, Moon was full at 97% in the high position, visibility was 10 miles Smoke. I decided to practice the GPS 29 approach into Susanville that was enroute to base. We were on a 5 mile final from the airport, descending though 7000 MSL at 95 knots of ground speed. One bird struck the right side front wind screen. I continued the instrument approach into Susanville. At 3 mile final descending though 6500 MSL at 95 knots ground speed. We struck a second bird on the right side front wind screen. I discontinued the instrument approach, slowed down to 80 knots ground speed, changed course and turned off my landing lights. A large amount of bird remains were found on the right side wind screen and upper wire cutter. Some blood and feather were found on the top forward cowling and the rotor head. I called our mechanic and asked him to inspect the helicopter. He came out to inspect the helicopter and I cleaned the wind screen and Cowlings. The aircraft was returned to service and we returned to base. NOTE: OWNER/ OPERATOR  AIR METHODS CORP. SOURCE  AMC BIRD/ WILDLIFE STRIKE REPORT.

Multiple aircraft were delayed approximately 5 minutes for FOD removal. No suspected loss of standard separation. A generic cautionary advisory for bird activity was on the ATIS. REMARKS: Impact point of 1st bird was at the upper left corner of the left windshield. The impact point of the 2nd bird was on the underside of the right wing root fairing. The aircraft departed Phoenix, AZ on 05/13/2019 at 6:50 pm Mountain time, landed the same date at Des Moines, IA at 11:22 pm Central time. The flying crew did not report a bird strike to any entity when departing, enroute, landing or after post flight inspection. The aircraft sat at Gate C6B at KDSM. The new outbound crew arrived and discovered the bird snarge while conducting the pre-flight inspection of the aircraft and reported the strike to American Airlines and Airport Operations on 05/14/2019 at 7:45 am . A Runway inspection was conducted without any evidence or remains being found of a bird strike. Reported result of inspection to American Airline operations. Since the strike was not reported by the flying crew, it is not determinable at this time where and when the strike occurred. FOUND AT KDSM.

"Double Bird Stike between gear up and 500 AGL. Takeoff normal, PF called gear up, moved selector to UP monitored until gear indicated UP, then opened Main Air Valves. I transitioned to scanning ahead looking Right to Left, just Left of the nose saw 2 bird shapes quite close, one dark the other not as dark probably diving away. Immediately after heard a noticeable thump ahead of the cockpit followed by a second not as loud thump. We both said birds. Then when the Main AIR valves opened we smelled something abnormal. PF reduced power. Alerted ATC of birdstrike and the request to return to land. Pressurization switched back to APU bleed from Engine Bleed, the abnormal smell quickly dissipated. Explained to passengers the issue of a precautionary landing. Stayed tower, entered Left downwind 32. KSTS airport ops did FOD check of runway, runway was clear. Performed necessary checklists. Landing was normal and uneventful. No abnormal engine indications were observed. After landing PF further explained the reason for return, Pax deplaned, went into terminal , baggage unloaded and taken to passengers. Evidence of a bird strike was smeared between the joint where the Radome and fuselage meet inline with the RH Pitot probe. Total flight time about 12 minutes. Airport OPS came and took feather sample. We did not clean the remains from the fuselage. MX found evidence of bird in LH engine duct. MCS LEASING INC   HAWKER 850XP. Tower called and reported a possible bird  strike on RWY 22R. Aircraft is a B717 tail number N965AT flight number DAL 1580 that parked at gate A11. Ops 331 sent to the runway and Ops 314 sent to the aircraft. 1525 Ops 331 picked up 2 small birds from the runway unknown type. 1526 Ops 314 found nothing on aircraft. Airfield Ops management made follow up calls and sent follow up emails the following day to gather more information due to internal records not indicating that this was a damaging strike. Airfield Ops Specialists stated that the initial call came through 20 minutes after the aircraft landed and that flight crew and maintenance were not available to speak to when they arrived at the gate. Delta Maintenance stated that they had no records of that aircraft having any bird strikes in the past two days and that no aircraft were out for service due to a bird strike. A barn swallow and a killdeer were found on inspection. Since the strike evidence was wiped off the aircraft before we could take a snarge sample, we can t be 100% sure on ID. Due to the number of Barn swallow strikes we have been receiving on RWY22R and the condition of the carcasses, we feel confident that the bird involved was the barn swallow rather than the killdeer. A separate and unrelated report for the killdeer will be filed. Right wing slat. WCAA NOTIFIED.

After departing Idaho Falls Regional Airport and passing through 8500â MSL, the Medical Crew and Pilot heard a loud bang and felt the aircraft shudder. The medical crew described it as if a piece of medical equipment had fallen to the floor making a loud bang and vibration. The pilot immediately disconnected the autopilot and took control of the aircraft to assess the controllability of the aircraft. The pilot initiated contact with ATC to let them know that they had hit something in flight and would need to return to the airport. Because the pilot had isolated the radios and the curtain was closed, the medical team did not know what was happening and felt something was wrong with the pilot. The pilot assured the medical crew he was fine and the aircraft was operating normally. The aircraft landed without incident and upon inspection found 5 bird strikes. 2 had hit the leading edge of the wing, 2 had hit the copilotâs windscreen and one had gone thru the propeller. The aircraft was placed out of service until a maintenance inspection could be completed. The medical crew coordinated and conducted patient transport back to Idaho Regional Medical Center. During take-off roll off Runway 7L, American Airlines Flt#5545 reported striking a large bird on Runway 7L between TWY N3 & N4. The aircraft aborted the take-off and returned to the gate. Airport Operations conducted a full sweep of Runway 7L and located an injured juvenile bald eagle and soft-shell turtle south of the center-line across from the 6K distance remaining sign on Runway 7L. The eagle appeared to be attempting to predate/investigate the turtle when it was struck by the aircraft. Airport Operations closed the runway and notified the Florida Fish & Wildlife Commission (FWC) of the strike to obtain clearance/authorization to remove the injured bird from the runway. FWC authorized Airport Operations to remove the injured bird from the runway and advised a FWC wildlife officer would be in contact for additional details regarding the injured bird and wildlife strike. Airport Operations spoke with officer J.P. (###) ###-#### who advised she was approximately 1hr away and enroute to collect the injured bird. Airport Operations collected the eagle and turtle; reopened the runway and returned control of the runway back to ATC. Airport Operations made contact with the crew of AA Flight 5545 to advise them of and confirm the aircraft sustained a wildlife strike. The crew advised they observed the eagle on the runway during the take-off roll but and heard a thump as they passed the birds location. Airport Operations and the flight crew conducted a visual check of the aircraft and located an area believed to be the point of impact. Airport Operations collected samples of possible snarge to send to the Smithsonian for confirmation. At approximately 1520 FWC arrived at the Airport to collect the injured bird for further care. The eagle appeared to be more active and aware while it was being loaded into the FWC vehicle. FWC requested the Airport to forward copies of the FAA and Airport wildlife strike report with any photos to FWC for records retention. End of Report.Right side fuselage under the pitot tube. The RSW ATCT notified Airport Operations that the flight crew for outbound Endeavor Air flight 3344, a Canadair Regional Jet (CRJ-900), reported a bird strike while on take-off run for Runway 06. Airport Operations inspected the runway and discovered the remains of five barn swallows as well as one tree swallow near the Taxiway A5 intersection. This led Airport Operations to register the strike as a triggering event due to all six birds being discovered within close proximity to one another. The flight continued to KLGA without incident. Arrived at aircraft N301PQ, flight 3344 that had just arrived at KLGA from KRSW and spoke with pilot who stated they received a bird strike upon takeoff from RSW, but could not specify the exact altitude or airspeed. Pilot stated that he reported the strike to air traffic control upon departure. Snarge sample was unable to be recovered. Flight departed RSW at 12:50 and arrived RWY 22 at LGA at 15:14. Barn Swallow, Tree Swallow.

Pilot report as follows: I was performing a checkride review with my student today. We had requested for a short approach to practice the power off 180 landing and when on the upwind leg we hit a bird. It was my students controls at the time and we were just initiating the turn to the crosswind leg. The bird appeared to be diving down in front of us when my student had promptly reacted to increase the pitch up before. We both reacted to pitch up resulting in only a slight hit on the nose wheel landing gear. I heard and felt a thump and estimating the birds projected path I figured he had hit the nose gear. We canceled the short approach and I asked the tower  if we could do a low pass for them to visually inspect our gear prior  to touching down. We returned for a full stop landing. On post flight inspection there was blood and feathers noticed on nose wheel tow bar attaching point. The plane was squawked and maintenance as well as safety department of Aviator College was notified. I had called tower to notify them and to see if any follow up was required.owner/operator   ARI BEN AVIATOR INC

After an uneventful flight from MCO to DFW, we were conducting a visual approach to runway 17C at DFW. I was the pilot flying. We completed the landing normally and taxied to the gate. All engine parameters were normal during landing and taxi in. We notified DFW Tower of the possible bird strike on taxi in, and they told us to confirm the strike with the tower once we had the airplane inspected by maintenance at the gate. Upon arrival at the gate, I contacted MCC via telephone through our dispatcher and made a logbook entry. The first officer also noted evidence of a bird strike (blood and feathers) above his window during the postflight walk around. I contacted DFW clearance delivery via radio to confirm with them that we found positive evidence of a bird strike.

At approximately 8PM EST, N885GT was conducting a practice instrument approach into JCA. After successful completion of the approach, the flight continued to make a routine touch and go. No wildlife or other obstructions were observed on or near the runway environment during approach. After the main wheels had touched down on the runway, three deer were observed running perpendicular to the runway a close distance in front of N885GT. Inspection of the arrival runway was completed both after report of strike on departure and after aircraft returned on next flight leg, but no other remains/evidence was found during either inspection. On Departure from Runway 09L in ATL we had a Bird strike. A few seconds before we had observed a flock of birds but was unable to avoid them. We heard 1 bang and that was all we heard. Checked engine instruments and all were normal with no fluctuations. We elected to continue the flight to Doha. Upon contacting Atlanta Center (KZTL) during the enroute climb, the controller gave us a phone number to call the Tower when we landed. I told the Controller we believed we only hit 1 bird but would know more once we landed back in Doha. After parking in Doha, I took a look at the Aircraft and observed only 1 bird strike just above the Captain s forward Window. An engineer was performing a post flight walk around so I pointed out the Bird strike to him. Tech log entry was made for the Bird Strike. I called the number given by the Center Controller and spoke with a from Atlanta Tower. **QTR756 (A7-ANJ) departed RWY 9L in ATL enroute to DOH when the crew reported a bird strike over the departure end of RWY 9L. ATL Airside Operations was notified of the report by ATCT and responded to the area. Upon inspection. three bird carcasses (European starlings) were located and removed from just west of the aiming point for RWY 27R. Assumed all carcasses involved in single incident. Departing aircraft did not report any in-flight issues due to the strike or indicate where on the airframe the strike occurred. Aircraft was at approximately 1200â and at a groundspeed of roughly 180kts when the event occurred.** MOR: Possible Bird Strike, QTR45C, A35K, KATL-OTHH, LC-3 (123.85). REMARKS: Jet Aircraft Maintenance notified Airport Operations that a bird strike was discovered on the right main landing gear of Sun Country flight 383. The remains of one Anhinga were removed from the landing gear. The pilots of flight 383 had left the area and therefore could not provide any further information on the strike; the RSW ATCT stated that the pilot reported birds at 600  while on final, but not an actual strike. Airport Operations inspected Runway 06 and did not find any further remains. DATABASE UPDATE ON 7.12.22. REVISED FROM FOUND KRSW TO APPROACH, 600 FEET, KRSW PER EMAIL FROM R DOLBEER ON 7.11.22 AS FOLLOWS: , I think we can reliably assign this strike to Approach at 600 feet at KRSW because 1) Pilot reported birds at 600 feet on final (landing gear would have been deployed), 2) anhinga was found in landing gear, 3) anhinga are found at KRSW (7 of the 62 anhinga strikes in NWSD are from KRSW; second only to the 13 at KMCO), 4) no anhinga was found on runway (which it would not be if it were stuck in landing gear; furthermore at 600 feet on final, aircraft would not have reached runway), and 5) the Pilot said âbirdsâ and anhinga typically fly in small flocks. I would put in Remarks âBased on pilotâs remarks to Tower of birds at 600 feet AGL on final to RSW and an anhinga found stuck to landing gear after landing, assume that the anhinga found in landing gear was struck on final at RSW. Based on Pilotâs remarks of âbirdsâ, assume 2-10 birds seen and 1 struckâ. If pilot had not reported âbirdsâ to tower at 600 feet on approach, I would not change this record. But the fact that the pilot felt the encounter on final approach was significant enough that he reported the birds to tower and an anhinga shows up in landing gear, makes it a compelling argument to me that this bird in landing gear was struck on final at 600 feet.

REMARKS: At approximately 2150 hours on 18 SEP 2023, while conducting a 100NM commercial night flight and established on RNAV 10 into KSAV, at approximately 1800 feet MSL, IP noticed what could have been a bird fly past the right side of the airplane. Once noticed, IP mentioned possible bird at altitude. After being instructed to conduct an option landing and turning to heading 120 degrees and climbing to 3000 feet MSL, at approximately 2149 hours and approximately 1200 feet MSL, IP heard what sounded like a slight audible thump, (SP was not aware after discussion at end of flight), thinking it could have possible been either a detonation or preignition on climb out, IP scanned all engine instruments to identify any abnormalities in order to determine if SP and IP need to return for a landing at KSAV or continue the flight. Once the assessment was concluded at approximately 2255 hours and it was determined the flight could be completed safely SP and IP continued the return leg back to KCRG. While on visual approach at approximately 5 NM North of KCRG for runway 32 at approximately 2240 hours and 2000 feet MSL, SP and IP noticed another possible bird fly past the right wing. After landing at approximately 2250 hours and taxing to parking at approximately 2255 hours, while IP was blocking in the airplane and the SP was securing the left wing with his white lens flashlight. SP mentioned to the IP that IP and SP may have had a bird strike. IP walked around the front of the airplane and with a white lens flashlight, inspected the possible bird strike location. Upon closer examination it was determined that there was a high probability of a bird strike just left (outside toward the wingtip as one would be facing to the front of the airplane from pilot seats) of the pitot tube. After the location was identified, SP and IP conducted a through 360 assessment of the airplane for any other issues. Once concluded, a final assessment was made and agreed on by both IP and SP that there were no other concerns. IP made a Mx report with a photograph of the bird strike location and submitted it for review and assessment by maintenance personnel. FLIGHT TRAINER LLC. On the above date and time, Airport Operations was notified by Ramp Control of a bird strike on N778SK, Canadair Regional Jet 700, operating as SKW3686 from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (KATL). SKW3686 landed on Runway 16 and taxied into Gate 3 of the Main Terminal. Airport Operations Coordinator S Reid reported to Gate 3 and observed snarge on the leading edge of the right wing. After speaking with the First Officer, it was noted that he heard the bird strike while descending on the approach for Westchester County Airport (KHPN). At the time of the bird strike, SKW3686 was approximately five (5) miles northeast of the airfield, at 3,000ft AGL, and at 250kts. The aircraft landed at 15:39L and a full-length surface inspection of Runway 16 was performed by Airport Operations Supervisor J Texidor at 15:41L with negative findings. A sample was taken and sent to the Smithsonian Institution Feather Identification Lab for positive species identification. USDA Wildlife Biologist S Beffre was notified. AIRPORT OPERATIONS NOTIFIED.

MOR Remarks: CNS47 DEPARTING RWY 27 HIT BIRD ON TAKEOFF ROLL, ABORTED TAKEOFF AND TAXIIED BACK TO THE RAMP. /Remarks from 5200-7 or other report: Report from pilot: During take-off roll on runway 27 at approximately 50 KIAS a small bird, which had been sitting on the runway, took flight as we approached but was unable to get out of the way and impacted the propeller. We heard the noise and visually observed the impact but it was a fairly small bird (sparrow?) and we did not feel any impact. It appeared that the bird hit the propeller above the spinner and continued past the cockpit windows. Immediately after I called out "bird strike, aborting take-off", applied moderate/light reverse thrust and light breaking as we still had several thousand feet of runway remaining. No unusual indications or vibrations were observed in the propeller or engine. After aborting we exited at taxiway F, taxied back to the FBO and shut down. There was an inbound aircraft on final (piston single, possibly a Cessna) which executed a go-around after our abort. Airport operations did an inspection of the runway but was unable to find any remains. Evidence of the bird strike was found on a propeller blade face approximately 4 inches from the spinner.BIRD REPORTED AS " POSSIBLY SPARROW".

My student, a passenger, and I were flying around 2700  during a night instruction flight. Approximately 9 miles out of Denton (KDTO), we heard a loud bang on the plane. I indicated to my student that we likely hit a bird. We did not see any wildlife approaching the aircraft. Since we were going to land in Denton as part of our training profile, we notified the tower about that and prepared to land. After landing, we inspected the plane and did not find any initial indications of a bird strike. Only after we checked the top of the wing did we see a strike of blood. The bird hit us on the area where the wing and windshield meet. No other indication of the bird was observed after we landed the plane for inspection. We did not have any bird remains on the plane (see picture). We only had a strike of blood over the wing. ARISPE AVIATION LLC. ONE PHOTO MOR: N739TS CHECKED IN APPROX 7NM NE REQUESTING PATTERN WORK. THE AIRCRAFT WAS APPROX 6NM NE AT 030 WHEN THE STRIKE OCCURED.

CREW REPTD FLYING THRU A FLOCK OF BIRDS THEN FELT VIBRATION IN #2 ENG. UNABLE TO SHUT DOWN ENG WITH FUEL CUTOFF LEVER. DISCHARGED FIRE EXTINGUISHER BOTTLE WHICH CAUSED ENG TO SHUT DOWN, BUT VIBRATION CONTD. UPON SEEING A/C WOULD NOT CLIMB OR ACCELERATE, PILOT RETRACTED FLAP AND GEAR. KEPT SPEED BELOW 180 TO REDUCE VIBRATION. A/C MADE EMERGENCY LDG AT JFK. FOUND 20X36 INCH DEPRESSION ON RT SIDE OF NOSE BEHIND RADOME. MAX DEPTH 3-4 INCHES. IMPACT MARKS ON RT WING AT 15 AND 18 FT OTBD FROM FUSELAGE AND BLOOD ON RT WING ROOT. RT ENG COWL RING WAS SPLATTERED WITH BLOOD AND 1 FAN BLADE WAS SEPARATED FROM THE FAN DISK AT THE ROOT. THE CONTAINMENT RING FOR THE FAN WAS PENETRATED BY A 9"X2" HOLE. ADDITIONAL HOLES IN ENG COWLING FWD OF CONTAINMENT RING. L SHAPED PENETRATION OF FUSELAGE. BLADE THAT PENETRATED FUSELAGE WAS NOT FOUND. ID BY SMITHSONIAN. PAX WERE BUSED BACK TO LGA AND PUT ON OTHER FLTS. FLT ATTENDANT REPORTED A LOUD BOOM AND ENTIRE A/C BEGAN TO VIBRATE EXCESSIVELY, WHOLE AFT SECTION FELT AS IF IT WAS ABOUT TO BREAK OFF. CAPT SAID THEY HAD LOST AN ENG. IT WAS LATER DETERMINED THAT 5 GEESE HAD BEEN STRUCK - TWO OF WHICH WERE INGESTED. THE AIRCRAFT WAS LATER  SOLD TO HELVETIC AIRWAYS. REMAINS OF 5 GEESE WERE FOUND ON THE RWY..

Leaving MHPR Rwy 35. On take off roll just prior to rotation. Encountered a large bird strike. The bird was ingested into the #1 engine. At the moment the bird was ingested by the motor there was a large thump sound. The aircraft yawed to the left. Then immediately regained centerline. At that point I looked to observe engine parameters. All were stable except the #1 engine EGT was stable at 890 degrees or so. This was substantially higher than the right engine. At that moment we were at rotation speed. I decided to continue the takeoff. There were no warning indications. The field elevation along with the runway length solidified my decision to continue. Once airborne we immediately got the smell of cooked carcass. Tower at that time asked us if we were ok. That there were flames that came out of the back of the #1 engine. As we monitored our instruments. The #1 engine EGT was running between 20 and 50 degrees warmer than the #2 engine. Once we reached a safe altitude the Fo and myself decided that it was best to declare an emergency and return to the field. At that time we climbed to 10,000ft. To remain clear of all terrain. Ran the applicable checklist. I informed dispatch, the Flight Attendants along with the passengers our intentions. We set up for the RNP35. Ran all the appropriate checklist. Landed w/o incident. CFR was standing by. Landed under max landing weight.
